HISTORY ASPECTS:
The Lockheed F-35B Lightning II, Bureau Number 169623, serves with Marine Fighter Attack Squadron 242 (VMFA-242) “Bats,” based at Marine Corps Air Station Iwakuni, Japan. In 2024, this fifth-generation stealth multirole fighter was regularly seen flying in its so-called “beast mode”—a configuration maximizing its external weapon loadout for high-intensity combat operations. VMFA-242 plays a key role in the Indo-Pacific region, providing forward-deployed airpower and rapid-response capability as tensions rise over territorial disputes and strategic rivalries in the South China Sea and Taiwan Strait.
The F-35B variant is distinct for its short takeoff and vertical landing (STOVL) capabilities, making it a perfect fit for Marine Corps expeditionary operations. Since transitioning to the F-35B in 2020, VMFA-242 has participated in numerous joint exercises and operational patrols under the U.S.-Japan security alliance, enhancing regional deterrence. While the squadron hasn’t been involved in large-scale conflict as of 2024, its deployments and training missions simulate combat readiness for near-peer threats, ensuring the U.S. maintains tactical superiority in any future confrontation.
The “beast mode” loadout demonstrated by aircraft 169623 at Iwakuni highlights the flexibility of the F-35B. Normally flown with internal weapons to preserve stealth, the jet can also be configured with six external pylons carrying bombs and air-to-air missiles when stealth is less critical. This configuration showcases its ability to shift from stealth penetration to full-force strike operations—a key feature in the evolving landscape of multi-domain warfare. VMFA-242, with its storied history dating back to WWII and the jet’s cutting-edge capability, symbolizes the fusion of heritage and future warfare.
This 1:72 scale model “beast mode” configuration, offers a dynamic snapshot of modern Marine Corps airpower. With meticulously rendered details, full external weapons loadout, and authentic squadron markings, it makes an eye-catching addition for collectors and enthusiasts of contemporary military aviation.

The Northrop T-38C Talon, tail number 65-10331, assigned to the 87th Flying Training Squadron (FTS) at Laughlin Air Force Base, is a modernized version of the legendary supersonic jet trainer. This specific aircraft, sporting the distinctive "FAIP" (First Assignment Instructor Pilot) scheme, reflects a tradition of excellence in pilot training within the U.S. Air Force. The FAIP scheme, featuring bold markings and high-visibility elements, distinguishes instructor aircraft flown by recent pilot graduates who return to serve as trainers. The T-38C has been integral in preparing student pilots for advanced fighter and bomber aircraft such as the F-22, F-35, B-1, and F-15E.
Although the T-38 itself was never used in combat, it played a vital support role by training thousands of U.S. and allied pilots since its introduction in the 1960s. The upgraded T-38C variant brought digital avionics, heads-up displays, GPS navigation, and improved cockpit ergonomics—transforming a Cold War-era design into a 21st-century training tool. At Laughlin AFB in 2021, aircraft 65-10331 operated under the Air Education and Training Command (AETC), helping maintain a steady pipeline of highly skilled pilots during a time of increasing global demand for air superiority and rapid-response capabilities.
The 87th FTS, known as the “Red Bulls,” is part of the 47th Flying Training Wing and boasts a proud lineage dating back to World War II. Their mission is to deliver world-class pilot training, and FAIP instructors—like those flying 65-10331—embody that mission with a blend of recent frontline insight and instructional rigor. Aircraft in the FAIP scheme stand as a badge of honor for these instructors, who shoulder the responsibility of shaping the next generation of combat aviators.

HISTORY ASPECTS:
The Messerschmitt Bf 109E-3 was the backbone of the Luftwaffe's fighter force during the early years of World War II, including the pivotal Battle of France and the Battle of Britain. Equipped with a Daimler-Benz DB 601 engine and armed with two 7.92 mm MG 17 machine guns and two 20 mm MG FF cannons, the E-3 variant represented a significant leap in firepower and performance compared to earlier models. Introduced in late 1939, it quickly proved itself as a formidable air superiority fighter and escort aircraft during Germany’s rapid advance across Western Europe.
In August 1940, Bf 109E-3 “Yellow 15” was flown by Karl Wolff, a pilot with III./Jagdgeschwader 52 (JG 52), one of the Luftwaffe’s most respected fighter units. During this period, JG 52 was stationed in northern France and engaged in intense operations over the English Channel as part of the Luftwaffe's air campaign against the United Kingdom. Wolff and his squadron were tasked with flying top cover for bomber formations, intercepting RAF fighters, and maintaining air superiority during the Battle of Britain, one of the most decisive air battles in military history. The aircraft bore the yellow tactical markings typical of Luftwaffe fighters at the time and carried distinctive unit insignia.
Although the Luftwaffe failed to achieve air superiority over Britain, the Bf 109E-3 earned a fearsome reputation for its agility, firepower, and speed. Pilots like Karl Wolff demonstrated the aircraft’s strengths in high-altitude dogfights against the RAF’s Spitfires and Hurricanes. While the Bf 109E was gradually phased out by newer variants, its impact during the early war years was profound, and its role in JG 52 laid the groundwork for the unit’s eventual status as the highest-scoring fighter wing in aviation history.
This 1:48 scale model is a must-have for aviation history enthusiasts and collectors. Expertly detailed with authentic markings and camouflage, it captures the spirit of the Battle of Britain era and brings to life one of the Luftwaffe’s most iconic early-war fighters.

HISTORY ASPECTS:
The F-15A Eagle 76-0111 of the 318th Fighter Interceptor Squadron (FIS), USAF, holds a unique place in aviation history as the only aircraft to successfully destroy a satellite in space using an air-launched missile. Assigned to McChord Air Force Base in Washington, 76-0111 was selected for the Anti-Satellite (ASAT) program in the mid-1980s, a top-secret initiative aimed at demonstrating the United States' capability to intercept and destroy enemy satellites during the Cold War. Equipped with the ASM-135 ASAT missile, the F-15A was specially modified to carry out this mission, including upgrades to its targeting systems and structural enhancements for high-altitude flight.
On September 13, 1985, Major Wilbert “Doug” Pearson piloted 76-0111 to over 38,000 feet above the Pacific Ocean near Vandenberg Air Force Base. At a steep 65-degree climb and traveling at Mach 1.22, he launched the ASM-135 missile, which successfully intercepted and destroyed the decommissioned Solwind P78-1 satellite orbiting over 300 miles above Earth. This event marked the first and only time a fighter aircraft achieved a kinetic kill against a satellite, demonstrating a powerful and controversial capability in space warfare. The test sent a strong strategic message during the Cold War and raised international concerns about the militarization of space.
Although the ASAT program was eventually shelved due to arms control concerns and diplomatic pressure, the legacy of 76-0111 and its historic mission endures. The aircraft continued to serve with the 318th FIS in a more traditional air defense role before eventually being retired. Today, the feat achieved by this Eagle represents a rare convergence of aerospace engineering, precision, and geopolitical tension—a moment when the limits of fighter jet capability reached into space itself.

Built in early 1940 by Vickers Supermarine, P9374 was assigned to No. 92 Squadron RAF during the early stages of the Battle of France. On May 24, 1940, Pilot Officer Peter Cazenove flew the aircraft on a combat mission over Dunkirk, providing air cover for the British Expeditionary Force as it faced encirclement by German forces. In the course of action, the Spitfire was hit by enemy fire and force-landed on the beach near Calais, where it remained buried in sand for more than 40 years.

The aircraft underwent a meticulous restoration to airworthy condition, completed in 2011, and was returned to flight wearing its original markings as it appeared during the Dunkirk operation. It became a flying memorial to both the pilots who flew these legendary machines and the thousands of troops evacuated under fire during Operation Dynamo.
While it saw only brief combat action, P9374's story powerfully illustrates the early and desperate days of WWII, when the RAF’s young pilots fought numerically superior forces with courage and determination. Its recovery and return to the skies made headlines and brought renewed attention to the sacrifices made during the Battle of France. Today, P9374 stands as a symbol of resilience—both of the aircraft itself and of the Allied efforts to turn the tide in Europe.

HISTORY ASPECTS:
The F-16C Fighting Falcon, tail number 85-474, served with the 706th Aggressor Squadron, part of the U.S. Air Force’s elite team responsible for simulating adversary air threats. Nicknamed "Rockslide," this jet was painted in an eye-catching two-tone gray and dark camouflage pattern designed to mimic enemy aircraft and tactics during high-end training exercises. The aircraft was stationed at Nellis Air Force Base, Nevada, and later operated in close coordination with the 926th Wing, enhancing the realism of Red Flag and other advanced aerial combat training events.
"Rockslide" played a key role in preparing U.S. and allied pilots for real-world engagements by flying as a “bad guy” in simulated dogfights and strike missions. Its purpose was not to deploy in combat zones directly but to provide aggressive training environments that reflected the challenges of contemporary threats, such as those posed by advanced Russian or Chinese fighters. The aircraft frequently participated in major exercises across the continental United States and abroad, pushing frontline squadrons to refine their tactics, survivability, and decision-making under pressure.
While F-16C 85-474 did not see traditional combat, its contribution to combat readiness was invaluable. Aggressor squadrons like the 706th exist to ensure U.S. and allied aircrews are battle-tested before ever facing a real adversary. "Rockslide," with its unique paint scheme and mission profile, became one of the more recognizable F-16s in the aggressor fleet, a symbol of the silent yet critical role played by mock-combat experts in U.S. air superiority doctrine.
This 1:72 scale model with authentic camouflage, tail markings, and fine detailing from canopy to weapons pylons. A perfect addition for collectors interested in adversary trainers, USAF history, or those who appreciate the behind-the-scenes heroes of modern air combat readiness.

ACME Trading is thrilled to present the latest 1:12 GT40 from our Masterpiece Collection! We are especially excited about this model as it completes the Masterpiece Collection's production of the four Ford GT40 MKIVs that competed in Le Mans 1967.
After Le Mans in 1966, Ford realized that the Mk II was reaching the end of its competitive life. It was heavy, and its aerodynamics were compromised. The decision was made to return to Le Mans with an all-new car incorporating the latest technology. With almost no regard to cost, this new GT40 was built around a reinforced J chassis powered by the same 7.0 L engine as the MKII. Excluding the drivetrain and suspension parts and brakes from the MKII, the new GT40 was totally different from the previous GT40s, using a specific, all-new chassis and bodywork. This resulted in one of the most beautiful and historic cars to ever race...the Ford GT40 MKIV.
New Zealander Denny Hulme and American Lloyd Ruby shared driving duties in the #4 Mark IV that was sponsored by Holman & Moody. During the race they were progressing nicely and, in fact, set the Le Mans top speed record at over 224 mph while rocketing down the famous Mulsanne Straight! Sometime after 9:15 PM, Ruby hit an oil patch left by a car ahead of him that blew its engine. Ruby slid off the track and into an embankment and unfortunately couldn't be repaired.

HISTORY ASPECTS:
The Air France Cargo Boeing 777-200LRF, registration F-GUOC, represents a modern era of air freight for one of Europe’s most historic airlines. Delivered in 2009, this aircraft was part of Air France’s strategic decision to transition from aging four-engine freighters like the 747-200F to the more fuel-efficient and environmentally friendly twin-engine 777 Freighter. Built for long-range performance, the 777F offers unmatched payload capacity and intercontinental reach, making it an essential asset in Air France’s global cargo operations.
F-GUOC quickly became a core component of Air France Cargo’s fleet, flying between major logistics hubs including Paris Charles de Gaulle, New York, Hong Kong, Dubai, and São Paulo. With the ability to carry over 100 metric tons of freight in a single flight, the aircraft supported everything from express shipments and pharmaceuticals to machinery and humanitarian aid. The combination of lower fuel consumption, high reliability, and the 777F’s proven GE90 engines allowed Air France Cargo to reduce operational costs while maintaining high levels of service and punctuality.
The aircraft proved its value during moments of global crisis, especially during the COVID-19 pandemic when dedicated cargo aircraft like F-GUOC became essential in transporting medical supplies, vaccines, and personal protective equipment. In the absence of passenger belly cargo space, the 777F fleet sustained global supply chains and supported emergency logistics needs. F-GUOC remains a vital part of the fleet, continuing to serve in a fast-paced global freight environment where speed, efficiency, and dependability are more important than ever.

The British Airways Airbus A380, registration G-XLEE, is one of twelve A380 superjumbos delivered to the airline as part of its long-haul fleet expansion. Delivered in 2014, G-XLEE represents the pinnacle of British Airways’ commitment to comfort, capacity, and global connectivity. As the world's largest passenger aircraft, the A380 brought new possibilities to high-demand routes, offering four cabin classes, including the flagship First, Club World (business), World Traveller Plus (premium economy), and World Traveller (economy), all with upgraded in-flight entertainment and space.
G-XLEE has been a familiar presence on British Airways’ flagship long-haul routes, connecting London Heathrow with major cities such as Los Angeles, Hong Kong, Johannesburg, and Singapore. Its ability to carry over 470 passengers with reduced emissions per seat made it an ideal choice for efficiently servicing heavily traveled international routes. The aircraft’s quiet cabin, expansive upper deck, and modern amenities quickly made it a favorite among frequent flyers and aviation enthusiasts alike. The A380 also allowed British Airways to consolidate flights on congested routes, maximizing slot usage at busy hubs like Heathrow.
Like the rest of the fleet, G-XLEE was temporarily grounded during the global COVID-19 pandemic, when long-haul travel demand plummeted. However, due to growing passenger demand post-pandemic and a shortage of long-haul aircraft, British Airways returned its A380s to active service, including G-XLEE. The aircraft continues to play a vital role in the airline’s post-COVID recovery strategy, helping to rebuild capacity on high-volume international routes. With its British Airways Union Flag tailfin and imposing double-deck design, G-XLEE remains a symbol of modern British aviation and global prestige.

HISTORY ASPECTS:
The Ferret Scout Car Mk.1/1 was a British armored reconnaissance vehicle developed in the early 1950s by Daimler as a successor to the wartime Daimler Dingo. Designed for speed, agility, and reliability, the Ferret served with the British Army and many Commonwealth nations for decades. The Mk.1/1 variant featured a fully enclosed turretless design, optimized for reconnaissance and liaison roles. Lightly armored but highly mobile, the Ferret was ideal for patrolling roads, screening movements, and providing forward observation without engaging in heavy combat. Its compact size and low profile made it an asset in both urban environments and rugged terrain.
C Squadron, based at Ludgershall, Wiltshire, in the 1980s, operated Ferret Scout Cars as part of the British Army’s reconnaissance and training units. During this period, the vehicle saw extensive use in NATO exercises across West Germany, reflecting the tense atmosphere of the Cold War. While the Ferret’s role in the 1980s was often centered on training and readiness, many Mk.1/1s in service had previously seen operational use in earlier conflicts such as the Malayan Emergency, the Aden Emergency, and peacekeeping missions in Cyprus. Its versatility allowed it to remain relevant in an era increasingly dominated by heavier and more advanced armored vehicles.
By the late 1980s, the Ferret Scout Car was gradually being phased out in favor of newer designs like the CVR(T) series, but it retained a special place in British Army history. For crews who operated it, the Ferret was a reliable workhorse—simple to maintain, rugged in the field, and surprisingly fast for an armored vehicle. Its service in both colonial conflicts and NATO defense scenarios demonstrated the adaptability of British armored reconnaissance doctrine over three decades.
This 1:35 scale model offers collectors a finely detailed piece of Cold War military history. From the precise replication of its armor plating to the accurate markings of the period, this replica is perfect for enthusiasts who value authentic representations of iconic reconnaissance vehicles that bridged the postwar and modern eras.

HISTORY ASPECTS:
The Messerschmitt Me 410A-1, Werknummer 10185, coded U5+KG, served with 16. Staffel of Kampfgeschwader 2 "Holzhammer" from its base at Amsterdam-Schiphol in October 1943. Developed as an improved successor to the troubled Me 210, the Me 410 featured more powerful Daimler-Benz DB 603A engines, refined aerodynamics, and improved handling. In its A-1 configuration, the aircraft was primarily used as a fast bomber, capable of carrying a variety of ordnance while retaining the ability to defend itself with heavy forward-firing armament, including 20 mm and 13 mm machine cannons.
In late 1943, 16./KG 2 was tasked with conducting fast, high-altitude bombing and intruder missions over England and the North Sea, targeting industrial centers, ports, and Allied shipping. The Me 410’s speed and firepower allowed it to evade or engage Allied fighters, but the growing presence of long-range escort aircraft, such as the P-47 Thunderbolt and P-51 Mustang, meant that these missions became increasingly dangerous. Despite this, crews flying the Me 410 from Schiphol managed to inflict damage on key supply routes and maintained a strong operational tempo through the autumn months.
The Me 410 also served in a reconnaissance and heavy fighter role, engaging in intercept operations against Allied bombers. By late 1943, some aircraft were fitted with additional weaponry, such as the 50 mm BK 5 cannon, to attack American B-17 and B-24 formations. Although powerful, the Me 410 was ultimately not fast or maneuverable enough to fully counter the Allies’ growing air superiority, and its losses increased into 1944. Nonetheless, examples like WNr. 10185 represent the Luftwaffe’s determined efforts to adapt and innovate under increasingly difficult wartime conditions.
This 1:72 scale model captures the sleek yet imposing lines of this versatile aircraft, complete with accurate KG 2 markings and wartime camouflage. Perfect for World War II aviation enthusiasts and collectors, it offers a historically rich addition to any display, honoring a Luftwaffe design that strove to balance speed, firepower, and adaptability in one formidable package.

HISTORY ASPECTS:
The Folland Gnat T.1 was a two-seat jet trainer developed from the lightweight Gnat fighter, designed to provide advanced training for Royal Air Force pilots transitioning to front-line fast jets. Introduced into RAF service in 1962, the T.1 variant replaced earlier jet trainers such as the de Havilland Vampire T.11, offering higher performance and handling characteristics closer to operational fighters. Compact, agile, and relatively inexpensive to operate, the Gnat became a crucial stepping stone in the RAF’s pilot training pipeline, preparing aviators for aircraft like the Lightning and Harrier.
In 1973, No. 4 Flying Training School at RAF Valley, Anglesey, Wales, operated the Gnat T.1 as part of its advanced training syllabus. The station was—and remains—a key hub for fast jet training in the UK. Student pilots at RAF Valley learned not only high-speed handling but also formation flying, aerobatics, and tactical maneuvers, skills essential for the operational squadrons they would soon join. The Gnat’s responsive controls and demanding flight characteristics were ideal for honing precision and discipline, producing some of the RAF’s most skilled aviators of the era.
While the Gnat T.1 itself did not participate directly in combat, its single-seat fighter counterpart served in several conflicts, most notably with the Indian Air Force during the 1965 and 1971 Indo-Pakistani Wars, where it earned the nickname “Sabre Slayer” for its success against Pakistan’s F-86 Sabres. The training work of the RAF’s Gnats ensured that British pilots were fully prepared to operate in the tense Cold War environment, ready for NATO rapid reaction duties in Europe and beyond. By the late 1970s, the Gnat T.1 began to be replaced by the British Aerospace Hawk T.1, but its legacy in shaping RAF jet training remained significant.
This 1:48 scale model faithfully recreates the sleek profile and vivid red-and-white training scheme of this iconic jet. With precise detailing, accurate proportions, and authentic RAF insignia, it’s a striking addition for collectors of classic British aviation and Cold War-era trainers.

HISTORY ASPECTS:
The Supermarine Spitfire Mk.I was the first production version of the legendary British fighter, designed by R.J. Mitchell and introduced to the Royal Air Force in the late 1930s. With its sleek elliptical wing, powerful Rolls-Royce Merlin engine, and eight .303 Browning machine guns, the Spitfire represented a quantum leap in fighter design and performance. It could reach speeds in excess of 350 mph, climb rapidly, and maneuver with exceptional agility, making it one of the most advanced fighters in the world at the time of its debut. Its arrival marked the beginning of a new era in British air defense, replacing aging biplane fighters and giving the RAF a modern edge against emerging threats.
No. 19 (Fighter) Squadron, based at RAF Duxford, was the first operational RAF unit to receive the Spitfire Mk.I, taking delivery of the type in August 1938. The squadron quickly transitioned from the Gloster Gauntlet biplane, learning to exploit the Spitfire’s speed, firepower, and handling. These early months were a period of intense training, as the squadron developed tactics and refined air combat maneuvers that would later be used in the desperate battles to come. Their aircraft bore the distinctive pre-war RAF markings and polished metal finish, soon to be replaced by camouflage schemes as the threat of war became imminent.
When the Second World War broke out in September 1939, No. 19 Squadron and its Spitfire Mk.Is were among the first to patrol British skies. They saw action during the early months of the conflict and later played a critical role in the Battle of Britain in 1940, defending the UK against the Luftwaffe’s onslaught. Although later versions of the Spitfire would feature more powerful engines and heavier armament, the Mk.I’s combination of speed, agility, and reliability made it a formidable opponent. Pilots of No. 19 Squadron were at the forefront of this fight, helping to secure the RAF’s hard-fought victory in one of history’s most decisive aerial campaigns.
This 1:48 scale model captures the aircraft at the dawn of its legendary service. Featuring finely rendered panel lines, accurate pre-war RAF insignia, and authentic squadron codes, this replica is a must-have for collectors and WWII aviation enthusiasts, offering a stunning tribute to the fighter that became a symbol of Britain’s defiance.

HISTORY ASPECTS:
The Supermarine Spitfire Tr.9 was a two-seat trainer variant developed from the combat-proven single-seat Spitfire, allowing pilots to receive advanced instruction in the handling of one of the most iconic fighters in aviation history. Built by converting late-war Mk.IX airframes, the Tr.9 retained the powerful Rolls-Royce Merlin 66 engine, giving trainees a true fighter’s performance while providing an additional cockpit for an instructor. This configuration made it an ideal advanced trainer for air forces transitioning pilots from basic flight school to high-performance frontline aircraft.
In 1951, the Irish Air Corps, or An tAerchór, received a small number of Supermarine Spitfire Tr.9 aircraft, including those assigned to B Flight at Baldonnel Aerodrome, Dublin. These Spitfires had originally served with the Royal Air Force before being refurbished for training duties. The Irish Air Corps had operated earlier marks of the Spitfire since 1947, acquired as part of post-war surplus sales, and the addition of the Tr.9 allowed for safer, more effective training for new fighter pilots. While the Republic of Ireland maintained a policy of neutrality during World War II and the Cold War, these aircraft ensured that the Irish Air Corps retained a cadre of highly skilled pilots capable of defending Irish airspace.
The Spitfire Tr.9 in Irish service did not see combat, but it played an important role in preserving the operational readiness of the Air Corps during a period of geopolitical tension. Its presence in Ireland’s inventory also reflected the country’s efforts to modernize and maintain a professional air defense capability despite limited resources. By the mid-1960s, the Irish Air Corps had retired the last of its Spitfires, replacing them with more modern jet trainers, but the Tr.9 remained a beloved symbol of Ireland’s post-war aviation heritage.
This 1:48 scale model reproduces the aircraft’s unique two-seat configuration, Irish roundels, and the distinctive markings of Baldonnel-based fighters in 1951. Perfect for collectors of classic warbirds and enthusiasts of Irish military history, this replica offers an authentic tribute to a rare and elegant variant of the legendary Spitfire.

The Boeing Chinook HC.1 ZA713/EN was part of the Royal Air Force’s No. 7 Squadron, a unit renowned for its heavy-lift helicopter operations in both peacetime and combat. Delivered in the late 1980s, this tandem-rotor workhorse was designed to transport troops, artillery, vehicles, and essential supplies into forward areas under challenging conditions. The HC.1 variant was the RAF’s initial version of the Chinook, featuring uprated engines, advanced avionics for the period, and the rugged airframe strength required for sustained operational tempo.
ZA713 saw notable action during Operation Granby—the UK’s codename for its role in the 1991 Gulf War—supporting coalition forces in the liberation of Kuwait. Deployed to the Gulf region in early 1991, it undertook a variety of missions, from ferrying Royal Marines and Special Forces to forward positions, to delivering ammunition, fuel, and humanitarian aid. The extreme heat, sand, and dust of the desert environment tested both crews and machines, but the Chinook’s proven reliability made it indispensable during the campaign. It also played a part in post-ceasefire operations, aiding in mine clearance support and the repatriation of displaced civilians.
The helicopter’s role in Operation Granby highlighted the RAF’s ability to project power and provide logistical lifelines in high-intensity operations far from home. No. 7 Squadron’s Chinooks became an enduring symbol of British air mobility during the Gulf conflict, with ZA713’s service exemplifying the adaptability and durability of the type. After the war, the aircraft returned to the UK, continuing to serve in training, domestic operations, and later deployments, contributing to the RAF’s global commitments.
This 1:72 scale model captures the exact configuration and markings worn during Operation Granby in May 1991, complete with Gulf War camouflage and operational detailing. Ideal for collectors of military aviation history, this replica pays tribute to one of the most versatile helicopters of the modern era, offering a striking display piece that tells the story of British air power in the desert.

HISTORY ASPECTS:
The Vought F4U-1A Corsair, flown by Major Gregory “Pappy” Boyington, became an iconic symbol of U.S. Marine Corps aviation during World War II. Known for its distinctive inverted gull wings, powerful Pratt & Whitney R-2800 engine, and exceptional speed and climb performance, the Corsair was a formidable fighter in both air-to-air combat and ground-attack missions. Boyington, commanding Marine Fighter Squadron 214 (VMF-214), famously nicknamed the “Black Sheep Squadron,” used the Corsair to achieve remarkable success against Japanese aircraft in the Pacific Theater, establishing himself as one of the most celebrated Marine Corps aces of the war.
VMF-214, led by Boyington, operated primarily from aircraft carriers and forward airstrips in the Solomon Islands and surrounding regions. The F4U-1A’s durability and firepower—armed with six .50 caliber machine guns—allowed Boyington and his squadron to excel in dogfights, often facing numerically superior Japanese forces. The Douglas SBD-3 Dauntless, Bureau Number 3232, marked S-7, was flown by Lieutenant (junior grade) Norman “Dusty” Kleiss of Scouting Squadron Six (VS-6) aboard the USS Enterprise during the Battle of Midway on June 4, 1942. The Dauntless was the U.S. Navy’s primary carrier-based dive bomber at the time, and despite being slower and less modern than some of its contemporaries, it had already proven its worth in the early months of the Pacific War. With a robust airframe, excellent diving characteristics, and a deadly 1,000 lb bomb load, the SBD became a decisive weapon in halting Japanese expansion across the Pacific.
During the climactic morning strikes of June 4, Kleiss and his fellow Dauntless pilots located and attacked the Japanese carrier Kaga. Diving steeply from altitude under intense anti-aircraft fire, Kleiss released his bomb with precision, scoring a direct hit. His attack contributed to the destruction of Kaga, one of four Japanese carriers sunk during the battle. Later that day, he struck again, delivering another devastating hit on the carrier Hiryu. Kleiss became the only dive bomber pilot at Midway to score confirmed hits on two different Japanese carriers in a single day, an achievement that cemented his place in aviation history.
The success of Kleiss and his squadron mates marked a turning point in the Pacific War. The Battle of Midway decisively shifted the balance of naval power, crippling Japan’s carrier force and giving the U.S. Navy the strategic initiative. SBD-3 BuNo. 3232, like other Dauntlesses at Midway, symbolized the courage and skill of U.S. naval aviators, demonstrating that well-trained pilots and reliable aircraft could overcome even the most formidable adversary. The Dauntless would continue to serve effectively until the end of the war, remembered above all for its vital role in securing victory at Midway.

Stationed in Italy, aircraft like 3U+AR provided bomber escort for raids against Malta and Allied shipping lanes, as well as ground-attack missions over North Africa. The aircraft’s range and versatility made it valuable in an environment where the Luftwaffe needed to project power across vast expanses of sea and desert.
During 1941, Bf 110E-2s flew extensively in support of Axis forces in North Africa, often launching from Sicilian and southern Italian airfields to strike British convoys resupplying Malta or reinforcing the Eighth Army in Egypt. Aircraft like 3U+AR faced increasingly dangerous opposition from RAF Hurricanes and Spitfires based on Malta, as well as long-range Bristol Beaufighters tasked with hunting Axis aircraft. This resulted in high losses, yet the aircraft remained in frontline service due to its ability to carry bombs, rockets, and to serve as a fighter-bomber—roles that single-engine fighters of the time struggled to balance.
The 7. Staffel of ZG 26, known as the “Horst Wessel” Geschwader, gained a reputation for resilience despite operating under difficult conditions. Bf 110 crews flew long missions over the Mediterranean, often battling both the enemy and mechanical strain from heat and dust in desert conditions. Specially weathered aircraft such as 3U+AR bore the visible scars of this harsh service environment—sun-faded camouflage, chipped paint, and sand erosion that reflected the relentless operations of 1941. The Northrop/McDonnell Douglas YF-23 was one of the most advanced fighter prototypes of its generation, developed for the U.S. Air Force’s Advanced Tactical Fighter (ATF) competition. PAV-2, serial number 87-0801, was the second prototype built and was nicknamed the “Gray Ghost” due to its overall light gray paint scheme. First flown in 1990, the aircraft was designed to push the boundaries of stealth technology, high-speed performance, and long-range air combat capabilities. Its sleek, diamond-shaped wings, V-tail configuration, and internal weapons bays made it one of the most futuristic aircraft of its time.
The YF-23 PAV-2 was equipped with three AIM-120 AMRAAMs and two AIM-9 Sidewinder missiles during weapons load demonstrations, showcasing its ability to carry a potent air-to-air arsenal entirely inside its fuselage to maintain stealth. Flight trials demonstrated that the Gray Ghost could achieve sustained supersonic speeds without afterburner (supercruise), a critical requirement for the ATF program. Its stealth characteristics were considered superior to its competitor, the Lockheed YF-22, and its aerodynamic design provided excellent high-altitude, long-range performance. Despite these strengths, the YF-23 was ultimately not selected for production, as the Air Force opted for the YF-22 (which evolved into today’s F-22 Raptor) due to cost, maneuverability, and development considerations.
Though it never saw combat, the YF-23 represents a pivotal moment in aviation history. The “Gray Ghost” embodied cutting-edge stealth and performance concepts that heavily influenced later aircraft design, including aspects of the F-35 Lightning II and next-generation fighter programs. Today, PAV-2 remains preserved as a remarkable artifact of what could have been the Air Force’s frontline fighter, symbolizing both the ambition and competitiveness of Cold War-era aerospace development.

In September 1940, JG 26 was deeply engaged in the Luftwaffe’s efforts to destroy the Royal Air Force and gain air superiority over southern England. Operating from bases in northern France, Perez and his comrades flew escort missions for German bomber formations targeting airfields, radar stations, and cities. The Bf 109E-3, known as the Emil, was the Luftwaffe’s frontline fighter at the time, combining speed, firepower, and agility to dominate early war skies.
Perez, like many young Luftwaffe pilots, faced formidable opposition in the skies above Britain. RAF fighters, including the Supermarine Spitfire and Hawker Hurricane, matched the Emil in performance, and the determined defense of Fighter Command turned the aerial campaign into a grueling contest of endurance. Missions across the Channel were particularly hazardous due to limited fuel reserves, forcing German pilots to balance aggressive combat tactics with the need to return to base. Within this high-pressure environment, “White 4” was part of the Luftwaffe’s sustained attempt to wear down the RAF during the climactic phase of the battle.
The Battle of Britain ultimately became the turning point of the air war. Despite the skill and bravery of pilots like Perez, the Luftwaffe was unable to achieve air superiority, and by October 1940 the campaign was effectively lost. The Bf 109E-3, however, earned a lasting reputation during this conflict as one of the finest fighters of its era, feared by opponents and respected by allies alike. For Perez and his Staffel, the autumn of 1940 represented both the peak of the Emil’s combat career and a pivotal moment in aviation history, where individual pilots shaped the course of the war in the skies.

HISTORY ASPECTS:
The Lockheed F-16C, serial number 86-0335, became one of the most recognizable aircraft of the 354th Wing, 18th Aggressor Squadron (AGRS) at Eielson Air Force Base, Alaska, thanks to its striking "Blue Splinter" camouflage scheme. In 2018, this jet was part of the U.S. Air Force’s premier aggressor unit, tasked with replicating potential adversary tactics, techniques, and aircraft during large-scale exercises. The Blue Splinter paint, inspired by Russian Arctic camouflage patterns, was designed not only to visually challenge friendly pilots but also to immerse them in realistic training environments, preparing them for combat against modern threats.
While the aircraft itself was not deployed to frontline combat zones during this period, its missions were no less critical. F-16C 86-0335 participated heavily in Red Flag-Alaska exercises, where it played the role of a simulated enemy fighter against U.S. and allied forces. By mimicking the tactics of Russian and Chinese aircraft, aggressors like the Blue Splinter trained pilots to adapt quickly, respond under pressure, and operate effectively in contested airspace. This role directly supported combat operations abroad, as pilots who trained against the 18th AGRS took those lessons with them into conflicts in the Middle East and other regions where U.S. airpower was engaged.
The presence of jets like 86-0335 ensured that the U.S. Air Force maintained a sharp tactical edge during a period of evolving global threats. By honing pilot skills in advanced air-to-air engagements, the 18th AGRS contributed indirectly to combat operations such as those in Iraq and Syria under Operation Inherent Resolve, where U.S. forces faced increasingly complex aerial and surface-to-air threats. In this way, even though 86-0335 never dropped bombs or fired missiles in combat, its contribution to readiness was essential to the success of frontline squadrons.
This 1:72 scale model perfectly recreates the bold Arctic-inspired camouflage and aggressive stance of one of the most iconic aggressor aircraft. A standout piece for collectors and aviation enthusiasts, it highlights the vital role of the 18th AGRS in shaping combat-ready pilots and adds a striking splash of color and history to any model aircraft collection.

HISTORY ASPECTS:
The Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-19PM was one of the Soviet Union’s first true supersonic interceptors, designed at the height of the Cold War to counter Western jet bombers and fighters. An evolution of the earlier MiG-19, the PM variant was fitted with a more advanced radar and armed exclusively with guided missiles, making it one of the first Soviet aircraft to abandon cannons in favor of all-missile armament. Aircraft such as Number 18 were part of the Soviet Air Defense Force (PVO), tasked with guarding Soviet skies against intrusions by NATO reconnaissance aircraft and potential nuclear-capable bombers.
The MiG-19PM entered service in the late 1950s and played a crucial role in the air defense posture of the USSR and its allies. Though never heavily engaged in direct combat under Soviet command, the aircraft did see operational use abroad through export to Warsaw Pact and friendly states. Variants of the MiG-19 were used by nations including East Germany, Poland, and Czechoslovakia, where they were positioned against NATO aircraft along the Iron Curtain. In addition, MiG-19s—including derivatives of the PM—were employed in conflicts such as the Vietnam War, the Indo-Pakistani wars, and Middle Eastern clashes, where they faced Western fighters like the F-4 Phantom and Mirage III.
As an interceptor, the MiG-19PM was intended to rise quickly, track intruders with its RP-5 Izumrud radar, and engage them with K-5 (AA-1 “Alkali”) air-to-air missiles. While the system had limitations in terms of missile reliability and radar range, the aircraft marked a major step in Soviet air combat doctrine, moving toward the missile age. Number 18 represents this transitional period of jet aviation, when speed, climb rate, and missile armament became the defining factors of an interceptor’s effectiveness.
This 1:72 scale model brings to life the sleek lines and Cold War character of one of the earliest supersonic interceptors. With finely detailed features, authentic Soviet markings, and an accurate representation of its missile-armed configuration, this replica is an ideal addition for aviation historians, Cold War enthusiasts, and collectors seeking a key piece of jet fighter evolution.

HISTORY ASPECTS:
The MiG-19PM, designated Number 335 in East German service, represented one of the first supersonic interceptors flown by the Luftstreitkräfte der Nationalen Volksarmee (LSK/NVA), East Germany’s air force during the Cold War. Introduced in the late 1950s, the MiG-19PM was a radar-equipped, missile-only interceptor derived from the base MiG-19 design, tailored specifically for air defense missions against NATO intruders. Aircraft like Number 335 formed part of East Germany’s frontline defense, stationed at key bases near the inner German border to respond rapidly to incursions by NATO reconnaissance aircraft and to reinforce the Warsaw Pact’s defensive air network.
The MiG-19PM was equipped with the RP-5 Izumrud radar and carried K-5 (AA-1 “Alkali”) guided missiles, reflecting the shift in doctrine from gun-based dogfighting to radar-guided missile interception. While its radar and missile systems had limitations compared to Western contemporaries, the aircraft gave East Germany a credible supersonic interceptor capability during a critical phase of the Cold War. Although Number 335 and its fellow East German MiG-19PMs did not see large-scale combat, they played an important deterrent role, frequently scrambled against Western reconnaissance flights along the Iron Curtain and maintaining constant readiness for potential conflict.
Beyond their service in East Germany, the MiG-19 family gained combat experience in the hands of other operators, including in the Vietnam War, Middle Eastern conflicts, and the Indo-Pakistani wars. These battles demonstrated both the strengths and weaknesses of the type, highlighting its excellent climb rate and speed but also the shortcomings of early missile technology. In East German service, however, the MiG-19PM was a stepping stone, bridging the gap between the first-generation MiG-15/17 fighters and more advanced interceptors such as the MiG-21, which soon replaced it in frontline units.
This 1:72 scale model captures the Cold War atmosphere with its authentic East German markings and sleek supersonic profile. Perfect for aviation historians, Cold War enthusiasts, and collectors alike, it offers a striking tribute to one of the Warsaw Pact’s early missile-armed interceptors, making it an essential addition to any model aircraft collection.

HISTORY ASPECTS:
The Arado E.555 I was one of the most ambitious designs proposed under Nazi Germany’s “Amerika Bomber” program during World War II. Conceived in the early 1940s by the Arado aircraft company, the E.555 I was a flying wing jet bomber intended to deliver long-range strategic strikes across the Atlantic, potentially reaching targets as far away as New York. Powered by six BMW 003 turbojet engines mounted at the rear of the fuselage, the aircraft promised high speeds and a range exceeding 4,000 miles, making it one of the most advanced concepts of its era. Its sleek, futuristic profile highlighted the rapid pace of German aeronautical innovation during the war.
Though never built, the E.555 I reflected Germany’s growing desperation as the tide of the conflict shifted. By 1943–44, Luftwaffe strategists recognized the need to strike Allied industry and morale far from the European theater, leading to proposals for a family of “Amerika Bombers.” The Arado project stood out for its radical design and theoretical performance, which surpassed most other submissions. Had it entered service, the bomber might have changed the strategic balance by forcing the United States to divert resources to homeland defense. However, technical limitations, resource shortages, and Germany’s deteriorating war situation kept the E.555 I on the drawing board.
Despite its lack of combat service, the Arado E.555 I has become one of the most iconic “Luft ’46” concepts—aircraft that never flew but captured the imagination of aviation historians and modelers alike. It represents both the visionary scope of late-war German aircraft design and the impracticality of such projects in a collapsing wartime economy. The E.555 I is often studied as an early precursor to postwar flying wing bombers, such as the Northrop YB-49 and the B-2 Spirit, making it a fascinating link between World War II experimental projects and modern stealth aviation.
This 1:144 scale model offers collectors a chance to own a piece of “what if” aviation history. With finely rendered contours of its flying wing design and precise attention to detail, it captures the daring vision of Arado engineers. Perfect for enthusiasts of experimental aircraft and Luft ’46 projects, this replica stands as a striking addition to any collection, blending history, imagination, and engineering ambition in miniature form.

The 1969 Pontiac GTO Ram Air IV was sold at the MECUM Kissimmee Summer Special 2023 auction on July 8th. This particular model, Lot S107, boasts a striking factory color combination of Carousel Red with a black interior. It's one of only 239 Ram Air IV GTO Judge hardtops produced with a 4-speed manual transmission in 1969. Under the hood, it features a powerful 400/370 HP Ram Air IV V-8 engine, ensuring an exhilarating driving experience.
Ordered with 15 factory options, including a Cordova vinyl top, bucket seats, power disc brakes, and variable-ratio power steering, it also features a Hurst-shifted Muncie M21 close-ratio 4-speed manual transmission, a 3.90 rear axle ratio with Safe-T-Track, and a Rally Gauge Package. Additional features like an in-dash electronic clock, pushbutton AM/FM radio with an 8-track player, and a remote driver's mirror add to its appeal. With only 88,802 miles at the time of auction, this comprehensively restored GTO is a rare and valuable piece of automotive history.

HISTORY ASPECTS:
The Aerolíneas Argentinas Boeing 737 MAX 8 registered LV-KEJ represents a modern leap in the airline’s fleet modernization program, designed to improve efficiency, passenger comfort, and operational range. As a next-generation narrow-body aircraft, the 737 MAX 8 features advanced engines, updated avionics, and improved aerodynamics, allowing it to operate longer domestic and regional routes with reduced fuel consumption. LV-KEJ has become a key asset for Aerolíneas Argentinas, linking major cities across Argentina and offering reliable service to neighboring countries in South America.
Throughout its operational service, LV-KEJ has been deployed on high-demand routes such as Buenos Aires to Córdoba, Mendoza, and Rosario, as well as international destinations including Santiago, São Paulo, and Montevideo. Passengers enjoy the aircraft’s quieter cabin, larger windows, and improved seating, while the airline benefits from the MAX 8’s efficiency and lower operating costs. Its performance and reliability have allowed Aerolíneas Argentinas to increase flight frequency and maintain punctual schedules, even on longer regional flights and routes with challenging operational conditions.
LV-KEJ also plays a symbolic role in Aerolíneas Argentinas’ commitment to sustainability and modern aviation. By integrating the 737 MAX 8 into its fleet, the airline not only enhances connectivity and passenger experience but also demonstrates its focus on environmentally responsible operations. The aircraft has quickly become a familiar sight in Argentine skies, contributing to the airline’s reputation for dependable and forward-looking air travel.
This 1:200 scale model beautifully captures the sleek lines, winglets, and distinctive livery of Argentina’s modern fleet. Perfect for collectors and aviation enthusiasts, it offers a highly detailed representation of one of the airline’s most advanced aircraft.

HISTORY ASPECTS:
The Flybe Dash 8 Q-400 registered G-ECOE was part of the airline’s modern turboprop fleet that helped redefine regional air travel in the United Kingdom and across Europe. Delivered during Flybe’s major expansion period, G-ECOE represented the airline’s shift toward fuel-efficient, high-performance aircraft capable of serving short-haul routes with lower emissions and excellent reliability. The Q400 quickly became the backbone of Flybe’s operations due to its speed, quiet cabin, and ability to operate from smaller airports where jet aircraft were less practical.
Throughout its service life, G-ECOE operated extensively across Flybe’s dense network, linking key regional destinations such as Manchester, Southampton, Belfast City, Birmingham, and Edinburgh. The aircraft played a vital role in connecting communities that relied heavily on regional air access for business, tourism, and essential travel. In addition, the Q400’s strong performance in challenging weather and its short-field capability made it ideal for Flybe’s northern and island routes, where runway lengths and adverse conditions posed operational challenges.
G-ECOE also flew during Flybe’s peak years, when the airline became Europe’s largest regional carrier by number of flights. Its livery, sporting Flybe’s signature purple tail and clean white fuselage, became a familiar sight at airports throughout the UK and beyond. Even after the airline’s operational changes and restructuring, the aircraft remained symbolic of Flybe’s important contribution to regional aviation, embodying its mission to provide fast, frequent, and affordable service to underserved markets.

HISTORY ASPECTS:
The American Eagle Saab 340B registered N389AE served as a vital link in the regional aviation network during the peak era of turboprop commuter service in the United States. Introduced to provide efficient, reliable transportation to smaller cities, the Saab 340B brought modern avionics, impressive short-field performance, and strong operating economics to the American Eagle fleet. N389AE became a familiar sight at hubs such as Dallas/Fort Worth, Chicago O’Hare, and Miami, where it connected travelers to destinations that larger aircraft could not economically serve.
Throughout its career, N389AE helped strengthen American Airlines’ regional presence by operating high-frequency routes that sustained business travel, local economies, and community access to the national air transportation system. The aircraft’s comfortable cabin layout, known for its quiet ride relative to earlier turboprops, made it especially valued among passengers traveling short segments. Its durability and dependable service record contributed to the Saab 340’s reputation as one of the most successful regional turboprops of its generation.
As regional aviation evolved and jet aircraft increasingly replaced turboprops, N389AE continued to serve until its retirement, marking the end of an era for many frequent flyers who fondly remembered the sound and character of the Saab 340B. Its service stands as a testament to the importance of regional aircraft in building the modern American Airlines network and supporting essential air connectivity across the country.
This 1:200 scale model captures the charm and character of this classic regional aircraft, featuring crisp details, accurate proportions, and the iconic early-2000s American Eagle livery. A perfect collectible for enthusiasts, it brings the nostalgia of turboprop travel directly to your display shelf.

HISTORY ASPECTS:
Eastern Air Lines’ Boeing 727-100 registered N8120N represents one of the most iconic eras in American commercial aviation. Introduced during the jet age boom, the 727-100 gave Eastern the perfect blend of performance and versatility—capable of operating from shorter runways while offering the comfort and speed of a modern tri-jet. N8120N served prominently throughout Eastern’s vast domestic network, connecting major hubs like Miami, Atlanta, and New York with emerging business and leisure destinations across the East Coast, Southeast, and Caribbean.
The aircraft became especially memorable in the polished-metal 1980s livery, a look that highlighted Eastern’s pride in its fleet while echoing the sleek, competitive style of the era. During this period, the airline continued to modernize its operations, and the 727 remained one of its most reliable workhorses. N8120N was part of the backbone of Eastern’s shuttle operations and high-frequency routes that catered to both business travelers and vacationers. Its distinctive three-engine silhouette and comfortable cabin design made it a favorite among frequent flyers.
As the airline industry shifted and larger, more fuel-efficient aircraft began to dominate, the early-series 727s gradually phased out of service. However, N8120N and its sister ships left an enduring legacy tied to Eastern’s golden years—an era defined by bold liveries, strong brand presence, and the unmistakable roar of the JT8D engines. For many aviation enthusiasts, the 727 in Eastern colors remains an unforgettable symbol of classic American commercial flight.
This 1:200 scale model beautifully captures the gleaming finish, sharp cheatlines, and signature tri-engine layout of one of the most recognizable aircraft in U.S. airline history. It’s a standout centerpiece for collectors who appreciate the elegance and nostalgia of Eastern’s legendary jet age.

HISTORY ASPECTS:
Supermarine Spitfire LF Mk IXe TE565 served with the Royal Air Force’s 310th (Czech) Fighter Squadron during the final phase of World War II, carrying the squadron code NN-N. The Mk IXe variant—equipped with the Merlin 66 engine and the “E-type” wing—was developed to counter the Focke-Wulf Fw 190, giving Allied pilots improved performance at low and medium altitudes. TE565 entered service at a time when the Czech-manned units of the RAF were heavily engaged in escort, interception, and ground-attack operations in support of the Allied push into occupied Europe.
During 1945, TE565 flew missions that contributed to the liberation of Nazi-occupied territories, including armed reconnaissance operations, fighter sweeps, and bomber escort sorties. The 310th Squadron played a key role in disrupting German transport networks, attacking enemy airfields, and providing top cover as Allied forces advanced through the Low Countries and into Germany. Although the war’s final months saw diminishing Luftwaffe resistance, the Spitfires remained active in safeguarding Allied troops from any remaining air threat. Aircraft like TE565 enabled Czech pilots—many of whom had fled their homeland after its occupation—to continue fighting for their country’s freedom while serving under the RAF banner.
After the war ended, TE565 was transferred to Czechoslovakia, where it became part of the newly reestablished post war air force. It served during the transitional years as the nation reorganized its military aviation capability before eventually retiring from operational duty. Today, TE565 is preserved at the National Technical Museum in Prague, standing as a powerful symbol of the Czech airmen who fought with extraordinary dedication in exile and returned home as liberators.
This 1:72 scale model captures the historic markings and elegant wartime lines of the legendary fighter. A perfect addition for collectors of WWII aviation or RAF history, it commemorates the skill and courage of the Czech pilots who flew it and brings an iconic museum aircraft into your display with exceptional detail.

HISTORY ASPECTS:
United Express’ CRJ550 registered N506GJ represents a significant evolution in regional air travel within the United States. Introduced as part of United Airlines’ strategy to enhance the passenger experience on short-haul routes, the CRJ550 became the world’s first 50-seat aircraft offering a true premium cabin layout. Operated by GoJet Airlines, N506GJ was among the early aircraft configured to meet United’s vision—featuring dedicated First Class seating, extra-legroom Economy Plus rows, and an enlarged galley to support improved onboard service. Its introduction marked a shift toward comfort-focused regional operations, especially on business-heavy corridors.
N506GJ quickly became a familiar sight at major United hubs such as Chicago O’Hare and Newark, where the CRJ550 fleet allowed United to offer consistent premium service on routes traditionally flown by smaller aircraft. The aircraft’s unique configuration also enabled compliance with scope-clause restrictions while still providing an elevated experience uncommon in the 50-seat category. From short Midwest hops to high-frequency East Coast connections, N506GJ played a key role in strengthening United’s competitive edge in the regional market.
Passengers appreciated the quieter ride, spacious overhead bins, and modern cabin ambiance that distinguished the CRJ550 from older regional jets. Over time, the aircraft became symbolic of United’s efforts to redefine expectations for regional air travel—merging efficiency with comfort without compromising operational flexibility. N506GJ continues to exemplify this commitment, remaining a valued workhorse across United Express routes.
This 1:200 scale model perfectly captures the aircraft’s sleek modern design, premium-configured layout, and sharp United livery. It’s an ideal addition for collectors who appreciate innovative aircraft that reshape airline service, bringing a standout regional jet into display-worthy detail.

HISTORY ASPECTS:
Lockheed C-130H Hercules serial 96-7325 has served with the United States Air Force’s Montana Air National Guard, assigned to the 120th Airlift Wing based in Great Falls. As part of one of the longest continuously operating C-130 units in the Air National Guard, this aircraft represented the Guard’s dual federal and state mission: providing tactical airlift for global operations while remaining ready to respond to emergencies at home. The C-130H variant brought improved avionics, reliability, and performance, making it a workhorse for medium-range airlift in demanding environments.
Throughout its service life, C-130H aircraft from the Montana ANG—including 96-7325—were routinely deployed in support of U.S. and coalition operations overseas. During the Global War on Terror, the 120th Airlift Wing flew missions connected to Operation Enduring Freedom in Afghanistan and Operation Iraqi Freedom, transporting troops, equipment, and humanitarian supplies into austere and often hostile airfields. These missions placed the aircraft in combat zones where flexibility, short-field capability, and rugged design were essential to sustaining frontline forces.
Beyond combat operations, 96-7325 also contributed to domestic and humanitarian missions, a hallmark of Air National Guard service. Montana ANG C-130s have been heavily involved in disaster relief following hurricanes, floods, and wildfires across the United States, as well as international humanitarian airlift missions delivering aid after earthquakes and other crises. This combination of combat support and lifesaving relief work highlights the enduring importance of the Hercules and the crews who flew it.
This 1:400 scale model in Montana Air National Guard markings faithfully recreates the distinctive look of aircraft 96-7325. Ideal for collectors of modern military airlift or Air National Guard history, it offers a compact yet highly detailed tribute to one of the USAF’s most versatile and battle-proven aircraft.

HISTORY ASPECTS:
The J-36 Stealth Fighter is widely understood as a next-generation Chinese combat aircraft concept associated with the People’s Liberation Army Air Force’s long-term modernization goals. Although not officially unveiled in full operational detail, the J-36 is commonly described by analysts as a sixth-generation or transitional platform emphasizing low observability, advanced sensor fusion, artificial intelligence–assisted decision support, and long-range strike capability. Its reported design philosophy reflects China’s focus on countering peer adversaries in highly contested airspace, particularly across the Western Pacific.
Rather than emerging from combat experience, the J-36 concept is rooted in lessons drawn from modern conflicts such as the Gulf War, Kosovo, and ongoing high-technology air operations observed globally in the 21st century. Chinese military doctrine increasingly prioritizes information dominance, networked warfare, and long-range precision engagement, all of which are believed to influence the J-36’s intended role. The aircraft is often linked in open-source assessments to future operations involving integrated air defense suppression, command-and-control disruption, and cooperation with unmanned loyal wingman platforms.
To date, there is no verified evidence that the J-36 has participated in any active conflict or combat deployment. Instead, it remains associated with developmental testing, simulations, and strategic planning rather than battlefield use. Its significance lies in what it represents: China’s ambition to field an air superiority platform capable of operating in environments shaped by stealth detection, hypersonic threats, and multi-domain warfare. As such, the J-36 occupies an important place in discussions of future air power rather than historical combat operations.
This 1:100 scale model captures the sleek, forward-looking design attributed to China’s next-generation air combat vision, making it an eye-catching centerpiece for collectors interested in speculative aviation, modern military strategy, and the future of stealth technology.

Aircraft like 810834 flew dissimilar air combat training missions in support of carrier air wings and fleet replacement squadrons, replicating the performance, tactics, and visual profiles of adversary aircraft encountered in conflicts such as the Gulf War, operations over the Balkans, Afghanistan, Iraq, and more recent global contingency planning scenarios.
By the 2020s, the Franken Tiger had become symbolic of the Navy’s ability to adapt legacy platforms to modern needs. Operating alongside newer adversary aircraft, the F-5F continued to provide cost-effective, high-quality training during exercises such as Red Flag, Weapons School support sorties, and fleet workups. Its two-seat configuration allowed instructor oversight and complex tactical instruction, ensuring that lessons learned from decades of air combat experience were passed to the next generation of fighter pilots. The aircraft’s service with VFC-111 concluded an era, as the Navy gradually transitioned to more advanced adversary platforms.

By April 1944, aircraft of the 388th BS were operating from Gusap Airfield in New Guinea, a strategically vital base supporting Allied advances toward the Philippines.
From Gusap, “The Hell’N Pelican II” took part in the New Guinea campaign, one of the most demanding theaters of the Pacific War. Crews flew hazardous missions at low altitude against Japanese supply lines, troop concentrations, and coastal shipping, often under intense anti-aircraft fire and challenging weather conditions. These operations were essential in weakening Japanese defensive positions and isolating enemy forces, contributing directly to the success of Allied ground offensives across New Guinea and nearby islands.
The A-20G Havoc played a broader role throughout the Pacific conflict, excelling in night intruder, strafing, and bombing missions. Aircraft like 42-86786 embodied the aggressive tactics adopted by Allied air forces, emphasizing speed, surprise, and precision. The ruggedness of the A-20 and the skill of its crews earned the type a formidable reputation, and units such as the 388th Bomb Squadron were instrumental in shifting the balance of air power in favor of the Allies as the war moved closer to Japan.

HISTORY ASPECTS:
The North American F-86E Sabre marked as 51-2752 is associated with Colonel George Andrew Davis Jr., one of the most celebrated American fighter aces of the jet age. Serving with the 4th Fighter-Interceptor Group and its 334th Fighter-Interceptor Squadron, Davis flew the F-86 during the height of the Korean War, a conflict that defined early jet-versus-jet air combat. The F-86E variant featured an all-flying tailplane, greatly improving maneuverability at transonic speeds and making it a formidable opponent against the Soviet-built MiG-15 over the infamous “MiG Alley” in northwestern Korea.
George Davis was already an experienced combat leader before Korea, having earned ace status flying P-47 Thunderbolts in the European Theater during World War II. In Korea, he quickly proved that experience and aggressive leadership translated into the jet age. Flying the Sabre with the 4th FIG, Davis led numerous combat patrols protecting UN bomber formations and hunting enemy fighters. He was officially credited with 14 aerial victories in Korea, becoming the leading American ace of the conflict. Aircraft 51-2752 is often linked to Davis in historical profiles, though the exact markings and scheme remain unconfirmed, reflecting the frequent repainting and unit-level variations common in combat conditions.
The F-86 Sabre itself became a symbol of United States air power during the Korean War, marking the first large-scale conflict dominated by jet fighters. Sabres of the 4th Fighter-Interceptor Wing clashed repeatedly with MiG-15s flown by Chinese, North Korean, and Soviet pilots, shaping air combat doctrine for decades to come. George Davis was killed in action in February 1952 while leading an attack against a superior number of enemy aircraft, an action for which he was posthumously awarded the Medal of Honor. His legacy is inseparable from the Sabre and the intense air battles fought over Korea.
This 1:72 scale model is an excellent addition for collectors who appreciate classic jet fighters and legendary pilots.   • HISTORY ASPECTS:
  • The Sherman Firefly Mk.IC was one of the most important armored fighting vehicles fielded by British and Commonwealth forces during the latter stages of the Second World War. Developed in response to the growing threat posed by heavily armored German tanks such as the Panther and Tiger, the Firefly was a modified American M4 Sherman fitted with the powerful British 17-pounder anti-tank gun. This weapon gave British armored units the firepower needed to engage enemy tanks at longer ranges, transforming the tactical balance on the battlefield.
  • A Squadron of the Coldstream Guards, part of the 5th Guards Armoured Brigade, operated Sherman Firefly Mk.IC tanks during the final phase of the Northwest Europe campaign. By 1945, the brigade was deeply involved in the Allied advance into Germany following the breakout from Normandy and the crossing of the Rhine. The Fireflys were typically integrated into troops alongside standard Shermans, providing overwatch and long-range anti-armor capability while working closely with infantry units of the Guards Armoured Division.
  • During the fighting in Germany, including operations such as the Rhineland battles and the final push toward northern Germany, Firefly crews faced entrenched German defenses, rearguard actions, and occasional armored counterattacks. The Coldstream Guards’ Fireflys played a crucial role in neutralizing remaining German armor and fortified positions, helping to secure key towns, road networks, and river crossings. These actions formed part of the broader Second World War European Theater conflict, culminating in the collapse of German resistance and the end of the war in Europe.
  • This 1:72 scale model markings captures a historically significant vehicle from the closing battles of World War II, making it a compelling addition for collectors who appreciate British armored history, late-war combat vehicles, and finely detailed representations of iconic battlefield machines.

  • “Carole,” a Sherman Firefly Mk.VC serving with C Squadron of the 13th/18th Royal Hussars (Queen Mary’s Own), was part of the 27th Armoured Brigade during the Normandy landings in June 1944. HISTORY ASPECTS:
The Curtiss P-40B/C Warhawk "White 47" was flown by Robert T. Smith, a skilled pilot of the 3rd Squadron "Hell's Angels," part of the legendary 1st American Volunteer Group, famously known as the "Flying Tigers." Operating under the Chinese Air Force, Smith and his squadron played a crucial role in defending Allied interests in the China-Burma-India theater. The P-40B/C Warhawk’s sturdy construction, six .50 caliber machine guns, and impressive diving speed made it a formidable opponent against the Japanese Zeroes, allowing pilots like Smith to execute daring tactics in both air-to-air combat and ground support missions.
Based in Burma, "White 47" saw extensive action during multiple sorties against Japanese aircraft and supply lines, often engaging in high-risk dogfights in challenging terrain and weather conditions. Smith’s precision and aggressiveness earned him a reputation as a formidable ace, contributing significantly to the AVG’s efforts to disrupt Japanese advances in the region. The P-40’s resilience under fire and its ability to sustain damage while remaining operational proved invaluable during intense engagements over Burmese jungles and airstrips.
The operational history of "White 47" highlights the courage, skill, and determination of the Flying Tigers, showcasing the P-40 Warhawk as a critical tool in countering Japanese air superiority in Burma. Smith’s accomplishments with the 3rd Squadron demonstrate the strategic and tactical impact that dedicated pilots and their aircraft had in the early years of the Pacific conflict, cementing the AVG’s legacy in aviation history.
This 1:72 scale model faithfully reproduces Robert T. Smith’s iconic aircraft, from the distinctive "Hell's Angels" squadron markings to the detailed Warhawk profile. A must-have for collectors and aviation enthusiasts, this model celebrates the daring exploits of the Flying Tigers and the vital role of the P-40 in shaping the aerial battles of Burma during World War II.

It supported both training and operational missions, providing transport for essential supplies, bridging logistical gaps, and facilitating rapid mobility in areas inaccessible to conventional trucks. Its rugged construction and all-terrain performance ensured that units could maintain supply lines under adverse conditions, often in areas where other vehicles would become bogged down or immobilized.
  • Beyond its operational use, the Stalwart Mk.2 became a symbol of innovation in military transport vehicles. Its combination of amphibious capability, load capacity, and off-road performance influenced later designs in military logistics and reinforced the importance of specialized vehicles for modern armed forces. Even after retirement from active service, the Stalwart Mk.2 remains a respected engineering achievement and a favorite among military vehicle enthusiasts.

  • HISTORY ASPECTS:
  • The Lockheed Hudson was a versatile American-built light bomber and coastal reconnaissance aircraft that saw extensive service during World War II. Developed from the Lockheed Model 14 Super Electra, the Hudson was adapted for military use by both the Royal Air Force and other Allied air forces. Its combination of speed, range, and payload capability made it a reliable platform for maritime patrol, convoy escort, and light bombing missions. The aircraft became particularly vital for anti-submarine operations in the North Atlantic, where it helped counter the persistent threat of German U-boats.
  • Hudsons were widely deployed in multiple theaters, including Europe, North Africa, and the Far East. In the Atlantic, they escorted convoys and conducted anti-submarine sweeps, often operating in harsh weather conditions while facing enemy fighters and submarines. In the Pacific and Southeast Asia, the aircraft performed reconnaissance, bombing, and ground attack missions, providing critical support for Allied ground forces and contributing to the broader strategic effort against Japanese forces. Its adaptability also allowed it to serve in intelligence-gathering and transport roles, highlighting its operational flexibility.
  • The Lockheed Hudson earned a reputation for being rugged and dependable, capable of returning safely even when heavily damaged. Its service with the RAF, RCAF, RNZAF, and other Allied air forces demonstrated the value of a multi-role aircraft in wartime operations. Pilots and crews came to rely on the Hudson’s robust construction and steady performance, which proved essential in both offensive and defensive missions across multiple continents.
  • This 1:72 scale model captures the iconic design and operational spirit of this historic aircraft. With accurate detailing of its twin-engine layout, reconnaissance equipment, and distinctive markings, it is a perfect addition for collectors and aviation enthusiasts seeking to honor the legacy of the Hudson and the vital roles it played during World War II.

  • The Royal Aircraft Factory B.E.2 is a British single-engine tractor two-seat biplane, designed and developed at the Royal Aircraft Factory. Most of the roughly 3,500 built were constructed under contract by private companies, including established aircraft manufacturers and firms new to aircraft construction.
  • This Royal Aircraft Factory BE2c plastic model kit comes with two paint scheme options, bringing variety to a popular design. With 54 well-engineered parts, this 1:72 scale kit is a joy to build.

• Brand new plastic model kit of WWII 3-Ton General Service and Troop Trucks (Level 2) 1/76 plastic model kit by Airfix.

  • HISTORY ASPECTS:
  • The WWII 3-Ton General Service (G.S.) and Troop Trucks were the backbone of Allied logistics, providing essential transport for soldiers, equipment, and supplies across multiple theaters of war. These vehicles were designed for rugged reliability, capable of carrying heavy loads over rough terrain while maintaining operational mobility. From fuel and ammunition to medical supplies and field kitchens, the 3-Ton trucks ensured that frontline units could remain supplied and combat-ready, regardless of the conditions they faced.
  • These trucks saw widespread use in nearly every major Allied operation of World War II, from the deserts of North Africa to the hedgerows of Normandy and the mountainous regions of Italy. Troop transport variants played a critical role in moving infantry efficiently to forward positions, enabling rapid deployments and supporting the mobility strategies that became essential to modern warfare. The G.S. trucks were often adapted to carry radio equipment, anti-aircraft weapons, and even towing light artillery, reflecting their versatility in diverse operational roles.
  • Beyond their combat service, 3-Ton G.S. and Troop Trucks were indispensable in supporting reconstruction efforts, field hospitals, and evacuation missions. HISTORY ASPECTS:
The Boeing CH-47C Chinook AE-520 holds a significant place in the annals of military history, particularly for its crucial role during the Falklands War in 1982. Operating under challenging conditions and unforgiving terrain, this iconic aircraft played a vital role in supporting British forces during the conflict.
As tensions escalated between Argentina and the United Kingdom over the Falkland Islands, the need for swift and effective transportation of troops, equipment, and supplies became paramount. The CH-47C Chinook AE-520 answered this call, embarking on daring missions to transport troops to remote and inaccessible locations. Its ability to carry heavy loads and navigate difficult environments proved indispensable in the logistical operations of the British forces.
The Chinook's versatility and adaptability were on full display during the Falklands War, as it executed a range of missions, including troop transport, medical evacuations, and resupply operations. Its presence significantly bolstered the operational capabilities of the British military and contributed to their success in the conflict. The CH-47C Chinook AE-520's participation in the Falklands War not only highlighted its prowess as a transport helicopter but also showcased the skill and determination of its crew.
This 1:72 scale model commemorates the historic role played by this aircraft during a pivotal conflict and pays tribute to the aircraft's legacy and the dedication of its crew. A must-have for military history enthusiasts, the model captures a moment in time when the Chinook proved its mettle under challenging circumstances, forever earning its place in the annals of aviation history.
